Before diving into the main question, it would be beneficial to establish some fundamental definitions and lemmas in topology and set theory. This will help us better understand and evaluate the proof provided.

Firstly, a *topological space* is a pair $(X,\scr T)$, where $X$ is any set and $\scr T$ is a collection of subsets of $X$, called open sets, satisfying three conditions: (i) $\emptyset$ and $X$ belong to $\scr T$; (ii) arbitrary unions of elements from $\scr T$ are also in $\scr T$; and (iii) finite intersections of elements from $\scr T$ are still in $\scr T$. When considering whether a particular collection of subsets forms a topology, these properties must be checked carefully.

Next, recall that a subset $S$ of $X$ is said to be *countable* if either $S$ is finite or there exists a bijective function between $S$ and the set of positive integers $\mathbb N$. Moreover, the *union of two sets*, say $A$ and $B$, is defined as $$A \cup B := \{x | x \in A \text{ or } x \in B\}$$ We assume Corollary [A], which states that the union of countably many countable sets is itself countable. Note that the empty set plays a role here since its cardinality is considered finite; therefore, it does not affect the corollary.

Now, let's analyze the proposed topology $(\scr T_2, X)$ based on our definition above. Consider the following:

1. Empty Set: Since $\emptyset \subset X$, by definition of $\scr T_2$, $X \backslash \emptyset = X$ should be countable. However, $X$ being infinite contradicts the assumption that $|X| > |\mathbb N|$. Therefore, $\scr T_2$ cannot contain only the empty set.
2. Whole Set: By construction, $X \in \scr T_2$ because $X \backslash X = \emptyset$, which is trivially countable.
3. Unions: Suppose $\{U_\alpha\} \subset \scr T_2$, meaning that $U_\alpha = \emptyset$ or $X \backslash U_\alpha$ is countable for every index value $\alpha$. Our goal is to show that $$\bigcup_{\alpha}^{} U_\alpha \in \scr T_2$$ If all $U_\alpha$ equal the empty set, then their union equals the empty set, which is clearly in $\scr T_2$. Otherwise, suppose at least one $U_\beta \neq \emptyset$ so that $X \backslash U_\beta$ is countable. Observe that for any other $U_\gamma$: $$(X \backslash U_\gamma) \backslash (X \backslash U_\beta) = U_\beta \cap U_\gamma \subset U_\beta$$ Thus, $(X \backslash U_\gamma)$ is contained within the countable set $(X \backslash U_\beta)$. Consequently, $(X \backslash (\bigcup_{\alpha}^{} U_\alpha)) = \bigcap_{\alpha}^{}(X \backslash U_\alpha)$ remains countable due to the intersection property of countable sets. Hence, $\bigcup_{\alpha}^{} U_\alpha \in \scr T_2$.
4. Intersection: Given finitely many sets $\{U_k\} \subset \scr T_2$, consider two cases: (a) All $U_k$ are equal to the empty set, implying their intersection is again the empty set ($\in \scr T_2$). (b) At least one $U_j \neq \emptyset$. Here, we have $$X \backslash \left(\bigcap_{k=1}^n U_k\right) = \bigcup_{k=1}^n (X \backslash U_k)$$ According to part 3., the right side of the equation represents the union of countably many countable sets ($X \backslash U_k$), making it countable. Therefore, $\bigcap_{k=1}^n U_k \in \scr T_2$.

Since $\scr T_2$ satisfies all four requirements listed earlier, it constitutes a proper topology on $X$.

cannabis industry, education, and health care are among the issues the Legislative Black Caucus of Maryland will focus on during the 2023 General Assembly legislative session
The caucus also seeks to establish concrete reforms that will remedy past loss and prevent any future damage. Examples of this include removing cannabis-related fines and fees and eliminating cannabis odor as a reason for law enforcement stops and searches. Profits from these businesses, they urge, need to be directed back into the communities that have been most affected by the drug's criminalization.
"We have a legal and the moral obligation to ensure that Black people across Maryland who have borne the brunt of the criminalization under prohibition are now put in a position where their damage is restored, and we create no more future harm," Carter, a Democrat, said.
Baltimore City Del. Stephanie Smith said making sure all students have access to a quality education and a need to support Black teachers and students are the overarching themes of the caucus' educational priorities.
Recruiting and retaining more diverse teachers at all levels is a key goal, as is strengthening the Maryland community schools program — which provides other services, such as job assistance, to students and their families — and doubling funding for a program providing tax credits for students borrowing to pay for their education. The caucus also wants more input into a plan to spend billions more on state schools, teacher training and other education programs.
"As we are implementing the Blueprint for Maryland's Future … we think that implementation requires the oversight of the Black Caucus," Smith, a Democrat said, "because one of the reasons why we established the Blueprint in the first place is that Black Marylanders were more likely to be attending underfunded schools."
Access to health care is also a priority.
"This session, we plan to save lives with the bills that we put forward," Prince George's County Democratic Del. Karen Toles said.
Goals include automatically enrolling those who receive Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits in Medicaid and expanding the availability of preventive care and testing. One bill Toles mentioned would require insurance companies in the state to cover biomarker testing, which can provide personalized information for treating cancer. Another bill being crafted in conjunction with the Susan G. Komen Foundation would eliminate out-of-pocket costs for people who need additional mammography not covered by their insurance.
Baltimore Democratic Del. Robbyn Lewis spoke of a large-scale public health overhaul for Black Marylanders that will assess the state's response to the COVID-19 pandemic, examine racial disparities in maternal mortality, and pay special attention to behavioral health and addiction, among other things caucus also supports elevating Black-owned businesses and taking steps to address racial wealth disparities, such as extending the Minority Business Enterprise Program. Another priority is earmarking $2,000,000 in the budget during fiscal years 2026 through 2031 to establish a tech diversity incubator.

Question: What is one of the key goals for improving access to health care, as mentioned by Karen Toles? Answer: Automatically enrolling those who receive SNAP benefits in Medicaid.

Philips adds 3 new software partners for hotel TVs

PPDS, the exclusive global provider of Philips Professional TV and Digital Signage products and software, has formed three new partnerships with hospitality industry property management system integrators Nonius, Nevotek and Imagine Soft, opening up more than one hundred additional PMS possibilities. 

As part of PPDS’ new “total solutions” strategy, these new collaborations—announced at this year’s AAHOA Convention and Trade Show—add control, management, communication and entertainment capabilities to Philips MediaSuite TVs, running on a bespoke interface that conforms to a customer’s needs. 

Nonius, Nevotek, and Imagine Soft join Impala and TigerTMS on PPDS’ list of partners and bringing the choice of PMS options to approximately 200. 

The new partnerships with Nonius (with 120+ million users worldwide and in 330,000 hotel rooms), Nevotek (with more than 3,000 hotels worldwide) and Imagine Soft (with 3,500 hotels worldwide and in 500,000 hotel rooms), help hoteliers communicate with guests and drive new revenue streams. 

The new platforms provide a variety of personalized services for guests, such as welcome messaging, bill viewing, native language selection, personalized offers and mobile check-in and checkout services.

With no additional hardware requirements for Philips MediaSuites needed, each of the partners’ platforms link seamlessly with the TVs’ existing OS. PPDS’ existing features and functionalities include the recently launched embedded Netflix solution, allowing guests to securely access their own Netflix account directly on the hotel TV, and the Chromecast built-in functionality, allowing guests to stream content (including apps) on the display directly from their device.

The platforms also let hoteliers offer tailored TV portals (T.V. channels, movies, sports), and integrate other third-party solutions like Apple TV, Sky, BT, VoD, as well as other live content feeds like news, weather, local attractions and transport information.

The problem asks for the locus of a point such that the sum of the squares of its distances from the sides of a unit square is 9. Here's the step-by-step solution:

1. **Define the Square and Coordinates**:  
   Let the square have sides at $ x = 0 $, $ x = 1 $, $ y = 0 $, and $ y = 1 $. A point $ (x, y) $ lies inside or outside this square.

2. **Distances to the Sides**:  
   - Distance to $ x = 0 $: $ x $  
   - Distance to $ x = 1 $: $ 1 - x $  
   - Distance to $ y = 0 $: $ y $  
   - Distance to $ y = 1 $: $ 1 - y $  

3. **Sum of Squares of Distances**:  
   The condition is:  
   $$
   x^2 + (1 - x)^2 + y^2 + (1 - y)^2 = 9
   $$

4. **Simplify the Equation**:  
   Expand and combine terms:  
   $$
   x^2 + (1 - 2x + x^2) + y^2 + (1 - 2y + y^2) = 9
   $$  
   $$
   2x^2 + 2y^2 - 2x - 2y + 2 = 9
   $$  
   $$
   2x^2 + 2y^2 - 2x - 2y - 7 = 0
   $$  
   Divide by 2:  
   $$
   x^2 + y^2 - x - y - \frac{7}{2} = 0
   $$

5. **Complete the Square**:  
   Rearrange and complete the square for $ x $ and $ y $:  
   $$
   (x^2 - x) + (y^2 - y) = \frac{7}{2}
   $$  
   $$
   \left(x - \frac{1}{2}\right)^2 - \frac{1}{4} + \left(y - \frac{1}{2}\right)^2 - \frac{1}{4} = \frac{7}{2}
   $$  
   $$
   \left(x - \frac{1}{2}\right)^2 + \left(y - \frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{7}{2} + \frac{1}{2} = 4
   $$

6. **Interpret the Result**:  
   The equation represents a **circle** with center at $ \left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right) $ (the center of the square) and radius $ \sqrt{4} = 2 $. Since the square's diagonal is $ \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414 $, the radius $ 2 $ is significantly larger, so the circle **contains the square**.

**Final Answer**:  
The locus is a circle with radius 2 centered at the square's center, which **contains the square**.

\boxed{\text{Containing the square}}

# Module in Abstract Algebra

In abstract algebra, a **module** is a generalization of a vector space, where the field of scalars is replaced by a ring. Modules retain the structure of abelian groups under addition and allow scalar multiplication by elements of a ring, subject to specific axioms.

---

### **Definition of a Module**
A **left R-module** consists of:
1. An abelian group $ (M, +) $,
2. A ring $ (R, +, \cdot) $ of scalars,
3. A scalar multiplication operation $ R \times M \rightarrow M $, denoted $ (r, x) \mapsto rx $, satisfying:
   - **Associativity**: $ (rs)x = r(sx) $ for all $ r, s \in R $, $ x \in M $,
   - **Distributivity over module addition**: $ r(x + y) = rx + ry $,
   - **Distributivity over ring addition**: $ (r + s)x = rx + sx $.

If the ring $ R $ has a multiplicative identity $ 1 $, and $ 1x = x $ for all $ x \in M $, the module is called **unital**.

---

### **Key Concepts**
- **Right R-modules**: Defined similarly, with scalar multiplication $ M \times R \rightarrow M $ (scalars act on the right).
- **Vector Spaces**: If $ R $ is a field, an $ R $-module is equivalent to a vector space over $ R $.
- **Bases**: Unlike vector spaces, modules may not have a basis (e.g., $ \mathbb{Z} $-modules like $ \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} $).

---

### **Examples of Modules**
1. **Abelian Groups as $ \mathbb{Z} $-modules**:  
   Every abelian group $ M $ is a module over the integers $ \mathbb{Z} $, where scalar multiplication is defined as:  
   $$
   nx = x + x + \cdots + x \quad (n \text{ times for } n \geq 0), \quad (-n)x = -(nx).
   $$

2. **Cartesian Products $ R^n $**:  
   For a ring $ R $, the set $ R^n $ is a module under component-wise addition and scalar multiplication.

3. **Smooth Manifolds**:  
   On a smooth manifold $ M $, the set of vector fields forms a module over the ring of smooth real-valued functions on $ M $.

4. **Matrix Modules**:  
   The Euclidean space $ \mathbb{R}^n $ is a left module over the ring of $ n \times n $ real matrices, with scalar multiplication defined by matrix multiplication.

5. **Ideals as Modules**:  
   Any left ideal $ I $ of a ring $ R $ is a left $ R $-module.

---

### **Submodules and Homomorphisms**
- **Submodule**: A subgroup $ N \subseteq M $ is a submodule if $ rn \in N $ for all $ r \in R $, $ n \in N $.
- **Module Homomorphism**: A map $ f: M \rightarrow N $ is a homomorphism if:  
  $$
  f(rm + sn) = rf(m) + sf(n) \quad \text{for all } r, s \in R, \, m, n \in M.
  $$

---

### **Alternative View: Representations**
A left $ R $-module can also be viewed as an abelian group $ M $ equipped with a **ring homomorphism** $ \rho: R \rightarrow \text{End}_{\mathbb{Z}}(M) $, where $ \text{End}_{\mathbb{Z}}(M) $ is the ring of group endomorphisms of $ M $. This homomorphism encodes the action of $ R $ on $ M $.

---

### **Why Modules Matter**
Modules allow the study of algebraic structures over rings, extending the theory of vector spaces. While vector spaces always have bases, modules may not, leading to richer and more complex structures. Key properties like torsion, projectivity, and injectivity are central to module theory and have applications in homological algebra, algebraic geometry, and beyond.

import mysql.connector
from mysql.connector import Error


def establish_database_connection(host: str, user: str, password: str, database: str) -> mysql.connector.MySQLConnection:
    """
    Establishes a connection to the MySQL database and returns the connection object.
    
    Args:
        host (str): The hostname of the MySQL server.
        user (str): The username for authentication.
        password (str): The password for authentication.
        database (str): The name of the database to connect to.
    
    Returns:
        mysql.connector.MySQLConnection: The database connection object.
    """
    try:
        connection = mysql.connector.connect(
            host=host,
            user=user,
            password=password,
            database=database
        )
        return connection
    except Error as e:
        print(f"Error connecting to MySQL Platform: {e}")
        raise


def create_database_cursor(connection: mysql.connector.MySQLConnection) -> Tuple[mysql.connector.MySQLConnection, mysql.connector.cursor.MySQLCursor]:
    """
    Creates a cursor for the given database connection and sets the timezone.
    
    Args:
        connection (mysql.connector.MySQLConnection): The database connection object.
    
    Returns:
        Tuple[mysql.connector.MySQLConnection, mysql.connector.cursor.MySQLCursor]: A tuple containing the database connection and cursor.
    """
    try:
        cursor = connection.cursor()
        cursor.execute("SET time_zone = '-07:00';")
        connection.commit()
        return connection, cursor
    except Error as e:
        print(f"Error creating cursor: {e}")
        raise


def update_last_updated_timestamp(connection: mysql.connector.MySQLConnection, cursor: mysql.connector.cursor.MySQLCursor) -> None:
    """
    Updates the last updated timestamp in the database.
    
    Args:
        connection (mysql.connector.MySQLConnection): The database connection object.
        cursor (mysql.connector.cursor.MySQLCursor): The database cursor object.
    """
    try:
        cursor.execute("SELECT updated_at FROM last_update;")
        current_timestamp = cursor.fetchone()[0]
        
        update_query = "UPDATE last_update SET updated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP WHERE updated_at = %s;"
        cursor.execute(update_query, (current_timestamp,))
        connection.commit()
    except Error as e:
        print(f"Error updating last updated timestamp: {e}")
        raise


def add_non_insert_query_to_stack(query: str, host: str, user: str, password: str, database: str) -> None:
    """
    Adds a non-insert query to the stack table in the database.
    
    Args:
        query (str): The SQL query to be added to the stack.
        host (str): The hostname of the MySQL server.
        user (str): The username for authentication.
        password (str): The password for authentication.
        database (str): The name of the database to connect to.
    """
    connection = None
    try:
        connection, cursor = create_database_cursor(establish_database_connection(host, user, password, database))
        insert_query = "INSERT INTO stack (query) VALUES (%s);"
        cursor.execute(insert_query, (query,))
        connection.commit()
        update_last_updated_timestamp(connection, cursor)
    finally:
        if connection and connection.is_connected():
            cursor.close()
            connection.close()


def add_insert_query_to_stack(query: str, values: Tuple[Any, ...], host: str, user: str, password: str, database: str) -> None:
    """
    Adds an insert query to the stack table in the database.
    
    Args:
        query (str): The SQL query to be added to the stack.
        values (Tuple[Any, ...]): The values to be inserted.
        host (str): The hostname of the MySQL server.
        user (str): The username for authentication.
        password (str): The password for authentication.
        database (str): The name of the database to connect to.
    """
    connection = None
    try:
        connection, cursor = create_database_cursor(establish_database_connection(host, user, password, database))
        insert_query = "INSERT INTO stack (query, val) VALUES (%s, %s);"
        cursor.execute(insert_query, (query, str(values)))
        connection.commit()
        update_last_updated_timestamp(connection, cursor)
    finally:
        if connection and connection.is_connected():
            cursor.close()
            connection.close()


def add_multiple_insert_queries_to_stack(query: str, values_list: List[Tuple[Any, ...]], host: str, user: str, password: str, database: str) -> None:
    """
    Adds multiple insert queries to the stack table in the database.
    
    Args:
        query (str): The SQL query template to be added to the stack.
        values_list (List[Tuple[Any, ...]]): The list of tuples containing the values to be inserted.
        host (str): The hostname of the MySQL server.

To solve the differential equation $ yx^2 \, dy - y^3 \, dx = 2x^2 \, dy $, follow these steps:

### Step 1: Rearrange the Equation
Start by moving all terms to one side:
$$
yx^2 \, dy - y^3 \, dx - 2x^2 \, dy = 0
$$
Factor terms with $ dy $:
$$
x^2(y - 2) \, dy - y^3 \, dx = 0
$$

### Step 2: Separate Variables
Rewriting to separate variables:
$$
\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y^3}{x^2(y - 2)}
$$
Separate variables:
$$
\left( \frac{y - 2}{y^3} \right) dy = \frac{1}{x^2} dx
$$

### Step 3: Integrate Both Sides
Simplify the left integral:
$$
\int \left( \frac{1}{y^2} - \frac{2}{y^3} \right) dy = \int \frac{1}{x^2} dx
$$
Compute the integrals:
$$
-\frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{y^2} = -\frac{1}{x} + C
$$

### Step 4: Rearrange to Match the Book's Form
Multiply both sides by $ y^2 $:
$$
- y + 1 = -\frac{y^2}{x} + C y^2
$$
Rearrange terms:
$$
1 - y + \frac{y^2}{x} = C y^2
$$
Multiply through by $ x $:
$$
x(1 - y) + y^2 = C x y^2
$$
Rearranged:
$$
(1 - C x) y^2 = x(y - 1)
$$
Let $ c = -C $, then:
$$
(c x + 1) y^2 = x(y - 1)
$$

### Final Answer
$$
(cx + 1)y^2 = (y - 1)x
$$
**Domain:** $ x \neq 0 $, $ y \neq 0 $, and $ y \neq 1 $ to avoid division by zero.

What is the largest number?  

The largest number in mathematics is **Graham's number**, which is the upper bound solution to an exotic problem in Ramsey theory. Unlike infinity, which is a concept rather than a number, Graham's number is an actual, albeit astronomically large, number.  

### Key Details:  
1. **Infinity is not a number**: It represents an unbounded quantity. You can always add 1 to any number, making it larger indefinitely.  
2. **Graham's number**:  
   - **Context**: It solves a problem in Ramsey theory asking for the smallest dimension $ n $ of a hypercube such that any two-coloring of its edges forces a planar complete graph $ K_4 $ of one color.  
   - **Magnitude**: Graham's number is so vast that it cannot be written down even if all the matter in the universe were converted to ink. For example, using the smallest measurable length (Planck length, $ 10^{-41} $ meters), the universe’s volume could not hold all its digits.  
   - **Comparison**: It dwarfs numbers like a googol ($ 10^{100} $) or a googolplex ($ 10^{\text{googol}} $).  

### Fun Fact:  
Mathematicians suspect the answer to the Ramsey problem might be as small as **6**, but Graham's number remains the largest number ever used in a mathematical proof.  

#### Answer:  
The largest number ever used in a mathematical proof is **Graham's number**.

Speaker John N. Stallone called the seventh meeting of the 38th Session to order at 3:00pm. Due to ongoing social distancing practices resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic, the meeting was conducted via Zoom. Speaker Stallone began by reminding Senators of the Zoom features to be used during the meeting.

APPRECIATION FOR SERVICE
Speaker Stallone reminded the Senate that President Michael K. Young and Provost Carol A. Fierke would both be leaving their posts as of December 31st. He first invited President Young to speak briefly to the Senate, who expressed his gratitude towards the faculty, especially during the challenges brought by the pandemic. In turn, on behalf of the whole Senate, Speaker Stallone shared appreciation for the work of the President. Provost Fierke was then invited to speak, but she had not yet joined the meeting.

GUEST SPEAKER
Speaker Stallone welcomed guest speaker Mr. Michael O'Quinn, Vice President for Government Relations and Strategic Initiatives. Mr. O’Quinn provided his view of what might be expected from the upcoming Texas Legislative Session, stating that the sessions are always unpredictable during normal times, and likely will be more unpredictable during the time of COVID.

- In the first two months, the Legislature is likely to meet two times a week, with the start of committee hearings occurring the end of January or early February.
- No big lobby days are scheduled, and no decision has been made if the sessions will be held virtually. There will likely be fewer bills this year.
- The budget will be a primary focus. Based on a recent revenue projection by the Comptroller, the state may be around $4 billion short for the biennium, but we won’t know where we stand until the House and Senate file their appropriation bills.
- Much attention is likely to be given to redistricting. The relationship between state and local governments, as well as gaming, are other expected issues.
- Texas A&M will work to get the additional funding received in the last legislative session. The goal is to receive funding to improve the faculty-to-student ratio impacted by the university’s growth, and the ask is $27.5 million.
- The Health Science Center has a separate budget request, as is customary with the state.
Mr. O’Quinn then took questions from the following Senators: Senator Dale Rice, College of Liberal Arts; Senator Lou Tassinary, College of Architecture; Senator Peter McIntyre, College of Science.

The full video recording of the meeting can be accessed on the Faculty Senate website: https://facultysenate.tamu.edu/Faculty-Senate-Meeting-Recordings.

Provost Carol Fierke joined the meeting, and Speaker Stallone invited her to speak to the assembly. She thanked the Senate and all faculty for their friendship and collaboration, and expressed pride in the way everyone met the challenges to keep the campus open throughout the fall semester. Speaker Stallone shared his thanks on behalf of the Senate, and wished her well at Brandeis.

Today's rockets are far too expensive and inefficient for large scale space colonization. Major problems are:

1. A lot of rocket fuel is used for launching more fuel into space, making fuel absurdly expensive.

2. Conventional rockets can only be used once, and space shuttles require expensive repairs and controls to be re-used.

To determine the number of ordered pairs $(b, c)$ satisfying the equation:

$$
a + (b \times c) = a \times b + a \times c
$$

we start by simplifying the equation. Rearranging terms and factoring, we derive:

$$
(b - a)(c - a) = a(a - 1)
$$

This equation implies that the product of two integers $(b - a)$ and $(c - a)$ equals $a(a - 1)$. The number of such ordered pairs $(b, c)$ corresponds to the number of ways to factor $a(a - 1)$ into two integers, considering both positive and negative factorizations.

---

### Key Observations

1. **Coprime Product Structure**:  
   The integers $a$ and $a - 1$ are consecutive, hence **coprime**. This allows us to compute the number of divisors of $a(a - 1)$ as the product of the number of divisors of $a$ and $a - 1$:

   $$
   \text{Number of divisors of } a(a - 1) = \text{fact}(a) \times \text{fact}(a - 1)
   $$

   where $\text{fact}(x)$ denotes the number of positive divisors of $x$.

2. **Inclusion of Negative Factors**:  
   For each positive factor pair $(d, e)$ such that $d \times e = a(a - 1)$, there are corresponding negative pairs $(-d, -e)$. Thus, the total number of ordered pairs $(b, c)$ is:

   $$
   2 \times \text{fact}(a) \times \text{fact}(a - 1)
   $$

---

### Special Cases

- **If $a = 0$ or $a = 1$**:

To solve the problem of finding the probability that two randomly selected individuals from a group of 7 are **not siblings**, we can follow a structured approach. Here's a detailed breakdown:

---

### **Step 1: Understand the Sibling Relationships**
- **4 people have exactly 1 sibling**: This implies there are **two pairs of siblings** (e.g., A-B and C-D).
- **3 people have exactly 2 siblings**: This implies there is **one trio of siblings** (e.g., E-F-G).

**Total sibling groups**:
- Two pairs: (A-B), (C-D)
- One trio: (E-F-G)

---

### **Step 2: Calculate Total Possible Pairs**
The total number of ways to choose 2 people out of 7 is calculated using combinations:
$$
\text{Total pairs} = \binom{7}{2} = \frac{7 \times 6}{2} = 21
$$

---

### **Step 3: Calculate Sibling Pairs**
We need to count the number of pairs that **are siblings**:
1. **From the two pairs**:
   - Each pair contributes 1 sibling pair.
   - Total from pairs: $2 \times \binom{2}{2} = 2 \times 1 = 2$

2. **From the trio**:
   - The number of ways to choose 2 siblings from 3 is $\binom{3}{2} = 3$

**Total sibling pairs**:
$$
2 (\text{from pairs}) + 3 (\text{from trio}) = 5
$$

---

### **Step 4: Calculate Non-Sibling Pairs**
Subtract the number of sibling pairs from the total pairs:
$$
\text{Non-sibling pairs} = 21 - 5 = 16
$$

---

### **Step 5: Compute the Probability**
The probability that two randomly selected individuals are **not siblings** is:
$$
\text{Probability} = \frac{\text{Non-sibling pairs}}{\text{Total pairs}} = \frac{16}{21}
$$

---

### **Alternative Direct Calculation of Non-Sibling Pairs**
You can also calculate non-sibling pairs by considering combinations between different groups:
1. **One from the first pair and one from the second pair**:
   $$
   \binom{2}{1} \times \binom{2}{1} = 2 \times 2 = 4
   $$
2. **One from a pair and one from the trio**:
   - For the first pair: $\binom{2}{1} \times \binom{3}{1} = 2 \times 3 = 6$
   - For the second pair: $\binom{2}{1} \times \binom{3}{1} = 2 \times 3 = 6$

**Total non-sibling pairs**:
$$
4 + 6 + 6 = 16
$$

---

### **Final Answer**
$$
\boxed{\frac{16}{21}}
$$

---

### **Key Takeaways**
- The problem hinges on correctly identifying the sibling groups (two pairs and one trio).
- Both methods (subtracting sibling pairs from total or directly counting non-sibling pairs) yield the same result.
- Always ensure that all combinations are accounted for without overlap or omission.

When Quarter Castle Publishing asked Isla Jane what had inspired her to write Swallowed, this is what she had to say.

I saw a video on YouTube by a man who had crashed his plane in the remote wilderness of Quebec. He survived because his plane had a parachute. I’d never heard of such a thing, so I did a little research on the subject and found CAPS, which stands for Cirrus Airframe Parachute System. As the website states, “The parachute system is designed to protect occupants in the event of an emergency by lowering the aircraft to the ground after deployment.”

Cool. Right? That’s what I thought.

Matt Lehtinen, the pilot who crashed and was stranded in the remote area of the province, shot a Vlog to capture his experience. He was rescued after only five hours but WOW, what an adventure.

My imagination absorbed the information and the energy from the video and the story took shape within minutes. It took much longer to write: 25 days.

import os
import sys
import fnmatch
import shutil

__all__ = [
    "delete_directory",
    "expand_path",
    "find_files",
    "get_resource_directory",
    "remove_duplicate_paths",
    "split_path",
    "open_universal_newline_file",

def delete_directory(directory_path: str) -> None:
    """Delete a directory and all its contents.

    Args:
        directory_path (str): Path to the directory to be deleted.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the path is a symbolic link or not a directory.
    """
    if os.path.islink(directory_path):
        raise ValueError(f"{directory_path} is a symbolic link.")
    if not os.path.isdir(directory_path):
        raise ValueError(f"{directory_path} is not a directory.")

    shutil.rmtree(directory_path)


def expand_path(path: str) -> str:
    """Expand a path to its absolute, normalized, and case-standardized form.

    Args:
        path (str): The path to expand.

    Returns:
        str: The expanded path.
    """
    return os.path.normcase(os.path.abspath(os.path.realpath(path)))


def find_files(
    paths,
    include_patterns=None,
    exclude_patterns=None,
    include_dir_patterns=None,
    exclude_dir_patterns=None,
    max_recursion_depth=None,
    include_directories=False,
    warn_on_mismatch=False,
) -> list:
    """Search for files matching specified patterns.

    Args:
        paths (str or list): Paths to search.
        include_patterns (str or list): Inclusion patterns for files.
        exclude_patterns (str or list): Exclusion patterns for files.
        include_dir_patterns (str or list): Inclusion patterns for directories.
        exclude_dir_patterns (str or list): Exclusion patterns for directories.
        max_recursion_depth (int): Maximum recursion depth.
        include_directories (bool): Include directories in results.
        warn_on_mismatch (bool): Print warnings for non-matching files/directories.

    Returns:
        list: List of matching paths.
    """
    if isinstance(paths, str):
        paths = [paths]
    if include_patterns is None:
        include_patterns = ["*"]
    if exclude_patterns is None:
        exclude_patterns = []
    if include_dir_patterns is None:
        include_dir_patterns = ["*"]
    if exclude_dir_patterns is None:
        exclude_dir_patterns = []

    found_paths = []
    for path in paths:
        if os.path.isfile(path):
            if _matches_patterns(os.path.basename(path), include_patterns, exclude_patterns):
                found_paths.append(path)
            elif warn_on_mismatch:
                sys.stderr.write(f"Skipping file {path}: no pattern match\n")
        elif os.path.isdir(path):
            if _matches_patterns(os.path.basename(path), include_dir_patterns, exclude_dir_patterns):
                if include_directories:
                    found_paths.append(path)
                _search_directory(
                    path,
                    include_patterns,
                    exclude_patterns,
                    include_dir_patterns,
                    exclude_dir_patterns,
                    max_recursion_depth,
                    include_directories,
                    warn_on_mismatch,
                    found_paths,
                )
            elif warn_on_mismatch:
                sys.stderr.write(f"Skipping dir {path}: no pattern match\n")
        elif not os.path.exists(path):
            sys.stderr.write(f"Warning: file does not exist: {path}\n")
        else:
            sys.stderr.write(f"Skipping non-file, non-directory: {path}\n")

    return remove_duplicate_paths(found_paths)


def _search_directory(
    directory_path: str,
    include_patterns: list,
    exclude_patterns: list,
    include_dir_patterns: list,
    exclude_dir_patterns: list,
    max_recursion_depth: int,
    include_directories: bool,
    warn_on_mismatch: bool,
    found_paths: list,
    current_depth: int = 0,
) -> None:
    """Recursively search a directory for files matching specified patterns.

    Args:
        directory_path (str): The directory to search.
        include_patterns (list): Inclusion patterns for files.
        exclude_patterns (list): Exclusion patterns for files.
        include_dir_patterns (list): Inclusion patterns for directories.
        exclude_dir_patterns (list): Exclusion patterns for directories.
        max_recursion_depth (int): Maximum recursion depth.
        include_directories (bool): Include directories in results.
        warn_on_mismatch (bool): Print warnings for non-matching files/directories.
        found_paths (list): List to store found paths.
        current_depth (int): Current recursion depth.
    """
    if max_recursion_depth is not None and current_depth >= max_recursion_depth:
        return

    for entry in os.scandir(directory_path):
        entry_path = entry.path
        if entry.is_dir():
            if _matches_patterns(entry.name, include_dir_patterns, exclude_dir_patterns):
                if include_directories:
                    found_paths.append(entry_path)
                _search_directory(
                    entry_path,
                    include_patterns,
                    exclude_patterns,
                    include_dir_patterns,
                    exclude_dir_patterns,
                    max_recursion_depth,
                    include_directories,
                    warn_on_mismatch,
                    found_paths,
                    current_depth + 1,
                )
            elif warn_on_mismatch:
                sys.stderr.write(f"Skipping dir {entry_path}: no pattern match\n")
        elif entry.is_file():
            if _matches_patterns(entry.name, include_patterns, exclude_patterns):
                found_paths.append(entry_path)
            elif warn_on_mismatch:
                sys.stderr.write(f"Skipping file {entry_path}: no pattern match\n")


def _matches_patterns(name: str, include_patterns: list, exclude_patterns: list) -> bool:
    """Check if a name matches any of the inclusion patterns and none of the exclusion patterns.

    Args:
        name (str): The name to check.
        include_patterns (list): Inclusion patterns.
        exclude_patterns (list): Exclusion patterns.

    Returns:
        bool: True if the name matches, False otherwise.
    """
    for pattern in include_patterns:
        if fnmatch.fnmatch(name, pattern):
            for excl_pattern in exclude_patterns:
                if fnmatch.fnmatch(name, excl_pattern):
                    return False
            return True
    return False


def get_resource_directory(package, *args) -> str:
    """Return the resource directory for a package.

    Args:
        package (module): The package module.
        *args: Additional path components.

    Returns:
        str: The resource directory path.
    """
    if getattr(sys, "frozen", False):
        pkg_root = os.path.dirname(sys.executable)
        if not os.path.isdir(pkg_root):
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"You are using pyinstaller and sys.executable={sys.executable} cannot be found."
                "To fix this, please put: sys.executable = os.path.abspath(sys.executable)"
                "at the beginning of your code."
            )
    else:
        pkg_root = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(package.__file__))
        if pkg_root.lower().endswith(".zip"):
            pkg_root = os.path.dirname(pkg_root)
    return os.path.join(pkg_root, package.__name__, *args)


def remove_duplicate_paths(path_list: list) -> list:
    """Remove duplicate paths from a list.

    Args:
        path_list (list): List of paths.

    Returns:
        list: List of unique paths.
    """
    seen_paths = set()
    unique_paths = []
    for path in path_list:
        expanded_path = expand_path(path)
        if expanded_path not in seen_paths:
            seen_paths.add(expanded_path)
            unique_paths.append(path)
    return unique_paths


def split_path(path: str) -> list:
    """Split a path into its components.

    Args:
        path (str): The path to split.

    Returns:
        list: List of path components.
    """
    path_components = []
    while True:
        head, tail = os.path.split(path)
        if not head or not tail:
            if head:
                path_components.append(head)
            if tail:
                path_components.append(tail)
            break
        path_components.append(tail)
        path = head
    path_components.reverse()
    return path_components


def open_universal_newline_file(path: str) -> object:
    """Open a file in universal newline mode if possible.

    Args:
        path (str): The path to the file.

    Returns:
        object: File object.
    """
    open_mode = 'rU' if sys.version_info < (3,) else 'r'
    return open(path, open_mode, encoding='utf-8')

Study Shows Calorie Restriction is Beneficial to Aging

6f0de3f5-020e-44aa-b77d-3b69a8f8b0cearticleimage.jpg

18 Jan 2017 --- A collaboration between two competing research teams-- one from the University of Wisconsin-Madison and one from the National Institute on Aging, has shown that restricting calories helps rhesus monkeys live longer and healthier lives. 

The findings were published in the journal Nature Communications.

The new report follows previous conflicted research results recorded by the two different research teams. 

In 2009, the UW-Madison study team reported significant benefits in survival and reductions in cancer, cardiovascular disease, and insulin resistance for monkeys that ate less than their peers. In 2012, however, the NIA study team reported no significant improvement in survival, but did find a trend toward improved health. 

“These conflicting outcomes had cast a shadow of doubt on the translatability of the caloric-restriction paradigm as a means to understand aging and what creates age-related disease vulnerability,” says Anderson, one of the report's corresponding authors.

Working together, the competing laboratories analyzed data gathered over many years and including data from almost 200 monkeys from both studies. Now, scientists think they know why the studies showed different results. 

First, the animals in the two studies had their diets restricted at different ages. 
Comparative analysis reveals that eating less is beneficial in adult and older primates but is not beneficial for younger animals. This is a major departure from prior studies in rodents, where starting at an earlier age is better in achieving the benefits of a low-calorie diet. 

Second, in the old-onset group of monkeys at NIA, the control monkeys ate less than the Wisconsin control group. This lower food intake was associated with improved survival compared to the Wisconsin controls. 

The previously reported lack of difference in survival between control and restricted groups for older-onset monkeys within NIA emerges as beneficial differences when compared to the UW-Madison data. In this way, it seems that small differences in food intake in primates could meaningfully affect aging and health.

Third, diet composition was substantially different between studies. The NIA monkeys ate naturally sourced foods and the UW-Madison monkeys, part of the colony at the Wisconsin National Primate Research Center, ate processed food with higher sugar content. The UW-Madison control animals were fatter than the control monkeys at NIA, indicating that at nonrestricted levels of food intake, what is eaten can make a big difference for fat mass and body composition. 

Finally, the team identified key sex differences in the relationship between diet, adiposity (fat), and insulin sensitivity, where females seem to be less vulnerable to adverse effects of adiposity than males. 

This new insight appears to be particularly important in primates and likely is translatable to humans. The key element of the report is that caloric restriction does indeed seem to be a means to affect aging. However, for primates, age, diet and sex must all be factored in to realize the full benefits of lower caloric intake.

To solve the integral $$\int (x^2 + 1)^3 \, dx$$, we analyze the problem step by step:

---

### **1. Why Substitution Fails Here**
Substitution is effective **only when the derivative of the substituted function appears in the integrand**.  
- Let $ y = x^2 + 1 $. Then $ \frac{dy}{dx} = 2x $, so $ dx = \frac{dy}{2x} $.  
- Substituting into the integral gives:  
  $$
  \int y^3 \cdot \frac{dy}{2x} = \frac{1}{2} \int \frac{y^3}{x} \, dy
  $$
  However, $ x $ is still present in the integrand. Since $ y = x^2 + 1 $, we can express $ x = \sqrt{y - 1} $, but this introduces a square root and complicates the integral further.  
  **Conclusion:** Substitution is not helpful here because the derivative $ 2x $ is missing from the original integrand.

---

### **2. Correct Approach: Expand the Binomial**
The integrand $ (x^2 + 1)^3 $ is a binomial raised to the 3rd power. Expand it using the **binomial theorem**:
$$
(x^2 + 1)^3 = x^6 + 3x^4 + 3x^2 + 1
$$

---

### **3. Integrate Term-by-Term**
Now integrate each term of the expanded polynomial:
$$
\int (x^6 + 3x^4 + 3x^2 + 1) \, dx = \int x^6 \, dx + 3\int x^4 \, dx + 3\int x^2 \, dx + \int 1 \, dx
$$
Compute each integral:
- $ \int x^6 \, dx = \frac{x^7}{7} $
- $ 3\int x^4 \, dx = 3 \cdot \frac{x^5}{5} = \frac{3x^5}{5} $
- $ 3\int x^2 \, dx = 3 \cdot \frac{x^3}{3} = x^3 $
- $ \int 1 \, dx = x $

---

### **4. Final Answer**
Combine all terms and add the constant of integration $ C $:
$$
\int (x^2 + 1)^3 \, dx = \frac{x^7}{7} + \frac{3x^5}{5} + x^3 + x + C
$$

---

### **Key Takeaway**
- **Substitution is only useful when the derivative of the substituted function is present in the integrand.**
- For integrals like $ \int x(x^2 + 1)^3 \, dx $, substitution would work (e.g., let $ y = x^2 + 1 $).
- Here, expansion is the most efficient method because the derivative $ 2x $ is missing.

import numpy as np
import sklearn.metrics as skmetrics

class ModelEvaluator:
    """
    A class that provides various methods to evaluate model performance using different metrics.
    """

    @staticmethod
    def calculate_log_loss(predicted_probabilities: np.ndarray, true_labels: np.ndarray) -> float:
        """
        Calculate the log loss between predicted probabilities and true binary labels.

        Args:
            predicted_probabilities (np.ndarray): Predicted probabilities.
            true_labels (np.ndarray): True binary labels.

        Returns:
            float: Log loss value.
        """
        return skmetrics.log_loss(true_labels, predicted_probabilities)

    @staticmethod
    def calculate_roc_auc(predicted_probabilities: np.ndarray, true_labels: np.ndarray) -> float:
        """
        Calculate the area under the ROC curve (AUC) between predicted probabilities and true binary labels.

        Args:
            predicted_probabilities (np.ndarray): Predicted probabilities.
            true_labels (np.ndarray): True binary labels.

        Returns:
            float: Area under the ROC curve.
        """
        return skmetrics.roc_auc_score(true_labels, predicted_probabilities)

    @staticmethod
    def calculate_accuracy(predicted_labels: np.ndarray, true_labels: np.ndarray) -> float:
        """
        Calculate the accuracy of predicted labels compared to true labels.

        Args:
            predicted_labels (np.ndarray): Predicted labels.
            true_labels (np.ndarray): True labels.

        Returns:
            float: Accuracy score.
        """
        return skmetrics.accuracy_score(true_labels, predicted_labels)

    @staticmethod
    def calculate_mean_f1_score(predicted_labels: np.ndarray, true_labels: np.ndarray) -> float:
        """
        Calculate the weighted mean F1 score of predicted labels compared to true labels.

        Args:
            predicted_labels (np.ndarray): Predicted labels.
            true_labels (np.ndarray): True labels.

        Returns:
            float: Weighted mean F1 score.
        """
        return skmetrics.f1_score(true_labels, predicted_labels, average='weighted')

    @staticmethod
    def calculate_precision(predicted_labels: np.ndarray, true_labels: np.ndarray) -> float:
        """
        Calculate the precision of predicted labels compared to true labels.

        Args:
            predicted_labels (np.ndarray): Predicted labels.
            true_labels (np.ndarray): True labels.

        Returns:
            float: Precision score.
        """
        return skmetrics.precision_score(true_labels, predicted_labels)

    @staticmethod
    def calculate_recall(predicted_labels: np.ndarray, true_labels: np.ndarray) -> float:
        """
        Calculate the recall of predicted labels compared to true labels.

        Args:
            predicted_labels (np.ndarray): Predicted labels.
            true_labels (np.ndarray): True labels.

        Returns:
            float: Recall score.
        """
        return skmetrics.recall_score(true_labels, predicted_labels)

    @staticmethod
    def calculate_rmsle(predicted_values: np.ndarray, true_values: np.ndarray) -> float:
        """
        Calculate the root mean squared logarithmic error between predicted and true values.

        Args:
            predicted_values (np.ndarray): Predicted values.
            true_values (np.ndarray): True values.

        Returns:
            float: Root mean squared logarithmic error.
        """
        log_pred = np.log(predicted_values + 1)
        log_true = np.log(true_values + 1)
        return np.sqrt(np.mean((log_pred - log_true) ** 2))

    @staticmethod
    def calculate_rmse(predicted_values: np.ndarray, true_values: np.ndarray) -> float:
        """
        Calculate the root mean squared error between predicted and true values.

        Args:
            predicted_values (np.ndarray): Predicted values.
            true_values (np.ndarray): True values.

        Returns:
            float: Root mean squared error.
        """
        return np.sqrt(skmetrics.mean_squared_error(true_values, predicted_values))

    @staticmethod
    def calculate_mse(predicted_values: np.ndarray, true_values: np.ndarray) -> float:
        """
        Calculate the mean squared error between predicted and true values.

        Args:
            predicted_values (np.ndarray): Predicted values.
            true_values (np.ndarray): True values.

        Returns:
            float: Mean squared error.
        """
        return skmetrics.mean_squared_error(true_values, predicted_values)

    @staticmethod
    def calculate_smape(predicted_values: np.ndarray, true_values: np.ndarray) -> float:
        """
        Calculate the symmetric mean absolute percentage error between predicted and true values.

        Args:
            predicted_values (np.ndarray): Predicted values.
            true_values (np.ndarray): True values.

        Returns:
            float: Symmetric mean absolute percentage error.
        """
        valid_indices = ~np.isnan(true_values)
        y_true, y_pred = true_values[valid_indices], predicted_values[valid_indices]
        smape = np.abs(y_true - y_pred) / (np.abs(y_true) + np.abs(y_pred))
        kaggle_smape = np.nan_to_num(smape)
        return np.mean(kaggle_smape) * 200

    @staticmethod
    def calculate_gini_coefficient(true_labels: np.ndarray, predicted_probabilities: np.ndarray) -> float:
        """
        Calculate the Gini coefficient between true labels and predicted probabilities.

        Args:
            true_labels (np.ndarray): True labels.
            predicted_probabilities (np.ndarray): Predicted probabilities.

        Returns:
            float: Gini coefficient.
        """
        return 2 * skmetrics.roc_auc_score(true_labels, predicted_probabilities) - 1

    @staticmethod
    def calculate_normalized_gini(predicted_probabilities: np.ndarray, true_labels: np.ndarray) -> float:
        """
        Calculate the normalized Gini coefficient between true labels and predicted probabilities.

        Args:
            predicted_probabilities (np.ndarray): Predicted probabilities.
            true_labels (np.ndarray): True labels.

        Returns:
            float: Normalized Gini coefficient.
        """
        if predicted_probabilities.ndim == 2 and predicted_probabilities.shape[1] == 2:
            predicted_probabilities = predicted_probabilities[:, 1]
        return float(ModelEvaluator.calculate_gini_coefficient(true_labels, predicted_probabilities)) / \
               ModelEvaluator.calculate_gini_coefficient(true_labels, true_labels)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Sample data
    y_true = np.array([0, 1, 1, 0, 1])
    y_pred_prob = np.array([0.1, 0.4, 0.35, 0.8, 0.9])
    y_pred_labels = np.array([0, 0, 1, 0, 1])

    # Evaluate metrics
    print("Log Loss:", ModelEvaluator.calculate_log_loss(y_pred_prob, y_true))
    print("ROC AUC:", ModelEvaluator.calculate_roc_auc(y_pred_prob, y_true))
    print("Accuracy:", ModelEvaluator.calculate_accuracy(y_pred_labels, y_true))
    print("Mean F1 Score:", ModelEvaluator.calculate_mean_f1_score(y_pred_labels, y_true))
    print("Precision:", ModelEvaluator.calculate_precision(y_pred_labels, y_true))
    print("Recall:", ModelEvaluator.calculate_recall(y_pred_labels, y_true))
    print("RMSLE:", ModelEvaluator.calculate_rmsle(y_pred_prob, y_true))
    print("RMSE:", ModelEvaluator.calculate_rmse(y_pred_prob, y_true))
    print("MSE:", ModelEvaluator.calculate_mse(y_pred_prob, y_true))
    print("SMAPE:", ModelEvaluator.calculate_smape(y_pred_prob, y_true))
    print("Gini Coefficient:", ModelEvaluator.calculate_gini_coefficient(y_true, y_pred_prob))
    print("Normalized Gini:", ModelEvaluator.calculate_normalized_gini(y_pred_prob, y_true))

UC Berkeley launches Center for the Science of Psychedelics

Share the story. Spark change.

This week, the University of California – Berkeley has launched the Center for the Science of Psychedelics.

The new research facility explores how we can use psychedelic substances (e.g., psilocybin, LSD, DMT, ayahuasca, and others) to better understand our brains, enhance well-being, and deepen spiritual insight. Its work will complement that of existing research centers focused on the topic – including those from Johns Hopkins University and Imperial College London – that combine psychedelic substances with psychotherapy to treat anxiety, depression, addiction, and a wide range of other mental illnesses.

“Some of these studies have produced striking results in cases that are otherwise resistant to more conventional medical treatment. This suggests that psychedelic compounds may offer new hope for people suffering from these disorders,” said Michael Silver, the Center’s inaugural director.

In addition to conducting research to better understand how psychedelics affect our brains and can provide practical benefits to our deepest personal challenges, the Center will also emphasize educating the public on how these substances can be used safely and to the great benefits of those who take it. For most Westerners, the use of such substances remains both illegal and taboo, often seen as deviant, unsafe, and irresponsible.

For me, this stigma is among the greatest and most tragic misperceptions of modern society. These substances are among the most powerful medicines known to humankind, frequently catalyzing life-altering experiences and prolonged behavioral change without the need for ongoing prescriptions. Perhaps this new center can help dispel this stigma and create a world where we are all encouraged to explore our internal worlds.

Key considerations when purchasing business IT

Computer equipment in a shop - key considerations when purchasing business IT.When you're buying new IT equipment for a specific reason - such as to replace a broken piece of hardware - it can be hard to think about its broader impact on your business

However, you’ll have to manage every piece of technology you buy – be it a cheap keyboard or super-expensive server. So, remember these key issues when purchasing new business IT:

  1. Set a budget. It's amazing how many businesses take the 'I'll replace it when it breaks' philosophy. With no IT budget in place, this approach isn't cost-effective - especially if it means you're unable to carry out key functions while you wait for new equipment to be delivered, checked, installed and configured. You must plan ahead, especially when it comes to equipment like servers, which can cost thousands of pounds.
  2. Match IT to your business needs. Your business needs should drive your IT requirements. Don't buy the latest equipment because it looks cool - buy it only if you need it. It's easy to waste money on technology without realising it, so get advice from a good IT supplier to ensure you buy appropriate kit. (As a side note, Microsoft found that the second highest activity for a computer after email was having it sit idle.)
  3. Think about maintenance. Don't underestimate the cost of ongoing management and maintenance. It's typical for a business to spend around 75% of its IT budget on maintaining existing technology, and only 25% on investing in new solutions. Often, a large proportion of that 75% is wasted by poor implementation and understanding of the equipment. Get it right first time, or you'll pay for the consequences over a lengthy period. Again, expert help is a good place to start.
  4. Go for managed services if you're outsourcing. Most IT support companies and suppliers offer 'managed services', which means they take care of all your day-to-day IT management. If your business can't afford a dedicated IT team, having your IT externally monitored and managed properly will stop lots of problems occurring in the first place. Managed services might cost a little more than an ad-hoc contract, but you'll see the value in reduced downtime and increased efficiency.
  5. Consider financing options carefully. Financing IT is no different to financing cars or sofas. Similar choices are available: instalments, delayed payment, etc. What's right for you will depend on your circumstances, but nowadays many businesses opt for a complete solution package. This means you buy hardware, engineering time, project management and support from one company, and pay a fixed monthly cost. You can also consider leasing equipment or shifting to cloud services, for which you usually pay a monthly subscription.
  6. Think about the cloud. If you plan to move to cloud services, bear in mind that you probably won’t require significantly powerful computer equipment, and can possibly reduce your on-site server requirements. This is because the processing will be carried out by the cloud supplier.
  7. Plan ahead. Maintaining an IT inventory can help you keep track of when you need to replace technology in your business. For instance, if you decide laptops should be replaced every three years, your inventory enables you to stick to this schedule. This can help you plan your IT purchasing in advance and ensure you have budgeted for all likely costs such as purchase, installation and training.
  8. Consider how you will dispose of old equipment. The Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE) Directive governs how you can dispose of IT equipment. Reputable suppliers will offer a disposal service - taking away your old equipment when they deliver your new pieces of kit.
  9. Keep an eye on new developments. The world of business IT changes fast, so try to keep track of the latest trends. For instance, it's easy to assume that you should replace your existing server with another one. However, you might be able to switch to cloud computing instead, replacing a complex piece of hardware with an external service for a manageable monthly cost. New technology can give you a competitive advantage. Ask your IT supplier for advice, and speak to other businesses to see what new technologies they've adopted.

from django.db import models
from typing import List

class Ingredient(models.Model):
    """
    A model representing an ingredient in the application.

    Attributes:
        name (str): The name of the ingredient.
        quantity (float): The quantity of the ingredient.
        unit (str): The unit of measurement for the ingredient.
    """
    name = models.CharField(max_length=255, help_text="The name of the ingredient.")
    quantity = models.FloatField(help_text="The quantity of the ingredient.")
    unit = models.CharField(max_length=50, help_text="The unit of measurement for the ingredient.")

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.quantity} {self.unit} of {self.name}"

class Recipe(models.Model):
    """
    A model representing a recipe in the application.

    Attributes:
        name (str): The name of the recipe.
        description (str): A detailed description of the recipe.
        serving_size (int): The number of servings the recipe yields.
        ingredients (ManyToManyField): A many-to-many relationship with Ingredient objects.
        updated_at (datetime): The datetime when the recipe was last updated.
        created_at (datetime): The datetime when the recipe was created.
        picture (file): An optional file field for uploading a picture of the recipe.
    """
    name = models.CharField(max_length=255, help_text="The name of the recipe.")
    description = models.TextField(help_text="A detailed description of the recipe.")
    serving_size = models.IntegerField(help_text="The number of servings the recipe yields.")
    ingredients = models.ManyToManyField(Ingredient, help_text="Ingredients required for the recipe.")
    updated_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now=True, help_text="The datetime when the recipe was last updated.")
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True, help_text="The datetime when the recipe was created.")
    picture = models.FileField(null=True, upload_to='recipe_pictures/', help_text="An optional file field for uploading a picture of the recipe.")

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        """Return the name of the recipe."""
        return self.name

    def update_recipe(self, name: str = None, description: str = None, serving_size: int = None) -> None:
        """
        Update the recipe details.

        Args:
            name (str, optional): The new name of the recipe.
            description (str, optional): The new description of the recipe.
            serving_size (int, optional): The new serving size of the recipe.
        """
        if name:
            self.name = name
        if description:
            self.description = description
        if serving_size:
            self.serving_size = serving_size
        self.save()

    def get_ingredient_names(self) -> List[str]:
        """
        Retrieve a list of ingredient names associated with the recipe.

        Returns:
            List[str]: A list of ingredient names.
        """
        return [ingredient.name for ingredient in self.ingredients.all()]

class Node:
    """
    A node in a doubly linked list.
    """
    def __init__(self, value: any):
        """
        Initializes a new node with the given value.
        """
        self.data = value
        self.next = None
        self.prev = None


class DoublyLinkedList:
    """
    A doubly linked list implementation.
    """
    def __init__(self):
        """
        Initializes an empty doubly linked list.
        """
        self.head = None
        self.tail = None
        self.size = 0

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        """
        Returns the number of elements in the list.
        """
        return self.size

    def add_to_front(self, value: any) -> None:
        """
        Adds a new node with the given value to the front of the list.
        """
        new_node = Node(value)
        if self.is_empty():
            self.head = new_node
            self.tail = new_node
        else:
            new_node.next = self.head
            self.head.prev = new_node
            self.head = new_node
        self.size += 1

    def add_to_back(self, value: any) -> None:
        """
        Adds a new node with the given value to the end of the list.
        """
        new_node = Node(value)
        if self.is_empty():
            self.head = new_node
            self.tail = new_node
        else:
            new_node.prev = self.tail
            self.tail.next = new_node
            self.tail = new_node
        self.size += 1

    def print_forward(self) -> None:
        """
        Prints the elements of the list from head to tail.
        """
        if self.is_empty():
            print("List is empty")
            return

        current = self.head
        elements = []
        while current:
            elements.append(str(current.data))  # Convert data to string for joining
            current = current.next
        print(" -> ".join(elements))
        print(f"Size of List: {self.size}")

    def print_backward(self) -> None:
        """
        Prints the elements of the list from tail to head.
        """
        if self.is_empty():
            print("List is empty")
            return

        current = self.tail
        elements = []
        while current:
            elements.append(str(current.data))  # Convert data to string for joining
            current = current.prev
        print(" <- ".join(elements))
        print(f"Size of List: {self.size}")

    def remove_from_front(self) -> None:
        """
        Removes the node at the front of the list.
        """
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Cannot remove from an empty list")
        if self.size == 1:
            self.head = None
            self.tail = None
        else:
            self.head = self.head.next
            self.head.prev = None
        self.size -= 1

    def remove_from_back(self) -> None:
        """
        Removes the node at the end of the list.
        """
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Cannot remove from an empty list")
        if self.size == 1:
            self.head = None
            self.tail = None
        else:
            self.tail = self.tail.prev
            self.tail.next = None
        self.size -= 1

    def is_empty(self) -> bool:
        """
        Checks if the list is empty.
        """
        return self.size == 0


# Example usage
if __name__ == "__main__":
    dll = DoublyLinkedList()
    dll.add_to_front(10)
    dll.add_to_front(20)
    dll.add_to_back(30)
    dll.print_forward()  # Expected output: 20 -> 10 -> 30
    dll.print_backward() # Expected output: 30 <- 10 <- 20
    dll.remove_from_front()
    dll.print_forward()  # Expected output: 10 -> 30
    dll.remove_from_back()
    dll.print_forward()  # Expected output: 10
    dll.remove_from_front()
    dll.print_forward()  # Expected output: List is empty

When a surgeon is prepping to carve into your body, he/she will sit down and plan every step of the procedure with assistants, practical nurses, surgical team technicians and the anesthesiologist. Having done a few procedures over time, they know they’ll need scalpels, metzenbaum scissors, sponges, betadine, lights, oxygen…well, the list goes on a bit. If it’s cardiac surgery, they know they’ll need rib spreaders. If it’s cranial, they’ll need a saw. Once the surgeon is scrubbed, draped and gloved, he or she will approach the table, call for a 10 blade and begin the dance to save your sorry butt. (I’m not sure what extra they’d need for butt surgery, but I’m sure there’s something.)

The point is, they have a template to work from. They’ve done enough surgeries to know all the basic things they’ll depend on once the operation begins. The tools they’ll need sit on what is called a surgical tray. What is your surgical tray? There are certain things you know you’ll need in nearly every piece of production. A few VO tracks, some music tracks, plus maybe an effects track or two. Then you have all of your “go-to” plugins like EQ, compression, reverb, noise reduction. Having everything laid out the way you like it, ready to simply start recording, fixing and mixing is smart and easy… once you design your template. When you sit down to start a new project, being able to have a familiar landscape for your work goes to more than just your comfort level. It allows you to gin things up without pondering how many VO/Music/Effects tracks you’re going to need, because everything is already laid out. Designing a template for session work is the ultimate shortcut.

The Ins and Outs of Your Template

Bussing is the fundamental building block of maintaining audio flow within your DAW. If you can NAME your busses, it will make life ever so much better. On my system, I have 64 busses, or 32 pairs available. Some systems have more, some less, depending on how robust your system is. I could have 128 busses, but I have yet to EVER need that many in broadcast production. If a bus is going to be used exclusively as a mono bus, you can name them individually, like Mic 1 and Mic 2, otherwise you can simply name bus pairs as designated stereo feeds. On my particular template I have them named Mixer, Compression, Flange, Reverb and, in a throwback mode, Bounce. (I don’t use that one anymore now that I can bounce directly to file.) It doesn’t matter what order they’re in. When you set an input or output on any fader or sub, it just has to be consistent.

Assuming you’re not a complete newbie, go back and look at what you’ve done previously. How many inputs did you use? How many sub-masters did you use? If you used multiple outputs, take that into account too. (I don’t, typically, but you gotta do you.) Take notes and decide what will be most helpful in this regard over the course of many, many sessions. Don’t forget that you can quickly add additional tracks, subs and masters when you’re in the throes of production. (Your own version of the surgical bone-saw.)

My own template has two input subs for one mic. Some of my clients want the super-duper-Z100-ultra-tight-hi-pass sound while others want it flat. They both get the same input assignment (there are no rules against that), but have different bus assignments on the output tabs. I USED to have another input sub that allowed me to quickly assign the input side to whatever device source material was on: CD, DAT, VCR, Turntable, etc., but I almost never use any of those sources anymore, so I deleted it. Almost everything I use for source material now comes in the form of a WAV or MP3 file. I download all my music directly to my hard drive and all my effects (both electronic and natural) are already stored in the system. I DO know several producers who mix music using a DJ system (turntable or CD) and have an input for that device.

I highly recommend having one sub-master for VO and another for music and effects, ALL stereo. You can divide the latter two into separate subs if that works better for you. Any processing you do on the VO sub will then be exactly the same across all of your VO tracks. Keep the processing on the music/FX sub to a minimum…for now.

Another sub-master you’ll want to consider is one dedicated to Reverb. Set the input to your reverb bus and the output to your mixing bus. Then drop your favorite reverb plug-in on the top insert. I use the WAVES Renaissance Reverberator plug-in because I do so many concert spots/promos. It gives me the most flexibility in designing the space involved (Madison Square Garden vs. a smaller venue like the Hammerstein Ballroom), and it has, by far, the easiest graphic display I’ve seen. A lot of my work doesn’t require any reverb at all, so it will sit there, unused most of the time, but having it constantly at the ready can speed things up when I do need it.

I also have an additional sub-master that you might find useful, perhaps using a different effect or even the same one. I “flange” my main VO, ever so slightly, without the wandering null point, by putting a delay plug-in on my “flange” sub and setting it to 20ms on one side and 40ms on the other, but I set the ‘wetness’ to 20%. This allows 80% of the signal to go straight through while adding the really short delay to the mix. Then, I set the output of my extra ‘flange’ sub to the main VO sub-master which is where ALL the voice tracks get compression and (sometimes) EQ. The other voice tracks? Read on.

Keeping Track Of Your Tracks

My VO tracks are all MONO, which gives me absolute control of pan-placement should I need it. I have a track for artist drops, one for listener/crazy drops, two for the main VO and one for a special hi-pass filter. The hi-pass track uses a 1kHz hi-pass EQ module and a compressor to squash the living hell out of the track before I send it to the VO sub-master. (The Hi-Pass track must use a ‘clipping’ type compressor like the WAVES L1 or you will get some awful distortion.)

Once created, I make sure I name each track so that anything recorded on that track will be properly stamped for future reference. When I look in the bin, the LAST thing I need to see is 45 files named Audio 1-01 thru 45 ad nauseam. Just double-click on the ‘scribble strip’ at the bottom of the fader and name it. I start each VO track name with a special character (√) so that all VO files will be grouped together in the bin. Then I add Artist, Listener, Main A and Main B, and finally Hi-Pass. I do the same ‘special character’ thing with music tracks, but with a different character (•). Of course, you can choose special characters that make sense to you. I start with 2 Music and 2 FX tracks (special character ƒ), all stereo, of course.

Now…Processing Your Music/FX

Remember how I said not to put much of any processing on your Music/FX sub-master? Glad you waited, ‘cause NOW we’re gonna do something fun! It’s called side-chain processing, and this alone might be worth the time you’ve put into reading thus far. It can be a REAL time-saver.

Open a comp/limiter on your music/FX sub-master and set the KEY Input to the VO sub-master. (Not all comp/limiters are created equal…at all. If there is no KEY Input button on the comp/limiter you’ve chosen, [check out the graphic] choose a different one because that one won’t work.) Once you’ve got the KEY Input selected, adjust the Threshold down to about -6db and set the Gain to about -6db. When you’re in play mode, the gain on the music/effects sub-master will automatically duck 6db whenever the VO is hot. When the VO track is silent, the music will play at full parity. Easy-peasy, right? (A LOT easier than manually ducking each music track!)

Clearly, you might need to make adjustments to the threshold and gain, depending on the thickness of the music, -6db is my ‘go-to’ start point. You should also keep the attack and release pretty loose just because it’ll smooth the transitions nicely. I find that if I keep the ratio fairly light, it will ultimately sound better too as it won’t make the music sound chunky, especially once you add your master compression.

Setting Up Your Yoda

Now your Master fader should have two plug-ins on it: EQ and compression. The master EQ is what you might want to have if you want to “color” the overall sound of the finished piece. Most of the time, if you’ve been careful up to the mastering stage, you won’t use it, but I keep it there just in case I want to brighten (or darken, I suppose…though I never have) the entire production.

The master compression is really just a control function, to deal with those moments when music and VO and effects all seem to hit at the same moment, driving a huge spike in gain overall. Some super light compression will deal with those oddities quickly and easily, giving the end product a nice, glossy finish, without pounding the hell out of the sound. Nobody likes clipping on music…trust me. An easy ratio of 2:1 will normally handle everything for you just fine. If the spot/promo is a bit more aggressive, you can always up it to 4:1 or just lower the threshold.

So…Now It’s Built

The way you save a template varies from system to system and DAW to DAW, so you’ll need to suss that out, but now that you have it, save it as your template. Every time you start a new project, you have all of your tools laid out, ready to rock. Within a couple of weeks, you’ll wonder how in the world you did everything on the fly before. You may find that you have to adjust your template from time to time, to take advantage of a new technique you’ve learned or a new plug-in you’ve acquired, but it will serve you well over time. Your production will start to grow in strength because you’re not as concerned about ‘how’ to get there as ‘why.’ Your consistency will jump and the powers-that-be will come to rely on you as a “fire-and-forget’ weapon in their quest for market dominance. Your stock will rise in the company, eventually resulting in a hefty raise and a lot of respect from your bosses and the radio community.

You’re welcome.

A couple of months ago, I noticed that my VO tended to taper off a bit toward the end of a phrase or sentence and was leaning toward putting a little more compression on my tracks. Instead, I started looking for something that wouldn’t glom up my VO (any more than what it is) and was delighted when I came across this beauty.
